title: Finding and fixing errors in algorithms
specPoints: **Identify common errors** in algorithms and **correct** them
Complete or refine an algorithm so that it meets its purpose
Links forward to 2.3.2 (syntax and logic errors) and 2.3.1 (input validation)
hook: This program is supposed to add up five prices and print the total. It prints 0 every time. Nobody typed anything wrong — every line runs. So what kind of mistake is it? (The `total = 0` is inside the loop.) Today: the mistakes that compile and run and are still wrong.

video.title: Two kinds of wrong: syntax errors and logic errors
video.brief: 4 minutes. Side by side: a program with a missing bracket (won't run — syntax) and a program that runs but resets `total` inside the loop (runs, wrong answer — logic). Then the 'top five' logic errors animated one by one with a trace table showing the symptom: off-by-one loop bound; `>` vs `>=`; `=` vs `==`; initialising inside the loop; wrong variable updated. Finish: 'you find syntax errors by reading the error message; you find logic errors by tracing'.

p: A **syntax error** breaks the rules of the language — a missing bracket, `endif` spelt wrong, a string without a closing quote. The program will not run and the interpreter tells you where. A **logic error** obeys the rules but does the wrong thing — the program runs and gives a wrong answer. Nobody tells you; you find it by testing and tracing.

list: **Off by one**: `for i = 0 to 9` instead of `1 to 10`, or `to 9` when you meant `to 10`. Symptom: one item missed or one too many.
**Wrong comparison**: `>` for `>=` (boundary value fails); `=` for `==` (assignment where a test should be).
**Initialising in the wrong place**: `total = 0` inside the loop resets it every time.
**Updating the wrong variable** or forgetting to update the loop variable in a `while` (infinite loop).
**Wrong operator or order**: `average = total / count` written as `total / count + 1`, or integer `DIV` where `/` was needed.
**Missing branch**: an `if` with no `else`, so one case produces no output.

explain.h: How to find them in the exam
p: Questions give an algorithm 'that contains an error' and ask you to **identify** the line and **correct** it, or give a purpose and ask you to **complete** missing lines. Method: read the purpose first; trace with one normal value and one boundary value; the row where your table disagrees with the purpose is the error. Then write the corrected line exactly — 'change line 3' is not enough on its own.

'Refine' means make it meet its purpose better without starting again: add input validation (reject a mark over 100), handle an edge case (an empty list), or use a sensible loop instead of a hard-coded number. Say what you changed and why it is an improvement.
A **syntax error** is a typing mistake that breaks the rules. The program will not run. The computer tells you where.
A **logic error** runs but gives the wrong answer. The computer does not tell you. You have to test it and trace it.

list: Loop starts or ends one number out.
`>` when it should be `>=` (or the other way).
`total = 0` inside the loop, so it keeps resetting.
A `while` loop where the variable never changes, so it never stops.
An `if` with no `else`, so sometimes nothing happens.

p: Read what the program is *meant* to do. Trace it with one normal number and one edge number (like 0 or the top limit). Where the table goes wrong is the error. Then write the fixed line.

keyterms.def: A mistake that breaks the rules of the language, so the program cannot run.
A mistake that lets the program run but produces the wrong result.
A loop or index that starts or ends one position too early or too late.
Improve an algorithm so it meets its purpose more fully, e.g. by adding validation or handling edge cases.

try.title: 1. Spot it, name it, fix it
p: Each algorithm has one logic error. For each: identify the line, name the type of error, write the corrected line.
try.code:
A)  Purpose: print numbers 1 to 10
    for i = 1 to 9
        print(i)
    next i

B)  Purpose: output "Adult" if age is 18 or over
    if age > 18 then
        print("Adult")
    endif

C)  Purpose: total of five inputs
    for i = 1 to 5
        total = 0
        total = total + int(input())
    next i
    print(total)

D)  Purpose: count down from 10 to 1
    n = 10
    while n > 0
        print(n)
    endwhile

try.title: 2. Complete it
p: This algorithm should output the average of the numbers in `scores`, but two lines are missing. Write them.

try.title: 3. Refine it
p: Take algorithm B (corrected). Refine it so that it also rejects ages below 0 or above 120 with the message "Invalid age". Write the whole thing and say in one sentence why this is a refinement.

try.title: 4. Debug for real
instructions: Work through the error-spotter. For each program, decide *before* running: syntax or logic?
Keep a tally. Which kind did you find harder to spot?

check.q: A program will not run and shows 'unexpected end of input'. This is a:
check.fb: It breaks the language rules, so it never runs.

check.q: `for i = 1 to 9` when 10 items were expected is a:
check.fb: Classic off-by-one; the symptom is one item missed.

check.q: A `while` loop never ends. Most likely cause:
opts: The condition variable is never changed inside the loop
check.fb: If nothing in the body changes the condition, it stays true.

check.q: How do you find a logic error?
opts: Trace the algorithm and compare with its purpose
check.fb: There is no message; tracing is the tool.

check.q: 'Correct the error' in an exam question needs:
check.fb: Write the fixed line; naming the line alone rarely scores.

exam.q: The algorithm below should output the largest number in the array. It contains an error. Identify the line containing the error and write a corrected version of it.
exam.code:
01 nums = [3, 8, 1, 9, 4]
02 largest = nums[0]
03 for i = 1 to 4
04     if nums[i] < largest then
05         largest = nums[i]
06     endif
07 next i
08 print(largest)
exam.commentary: Both marks need the correct line **and** the corrected code. Students often spot the symptom ('it finds the smallest') but write 'change < to >' without the full line — that is accepted here, but writing the full line is safer. Tracing with the first two values (3 then 8) shows the error immediately.

exam.q: An algorithm asks the user to enter a percentage and stores it. Describe **two** refinements that would make the algorithm more robust.
model: Check the value is within range 0 to 100 and ask again / show an error if not (1 + 1 for how). Check the input is a whole number / numeric, not text, before storing it (1 + 1 for how).
exam.commentary: Each refinement is 'what' plus 'how'. Range check and type check are the two the mark scheme expects; a presence check (not blank) also scores. Writing the check as pseudocode is fine but not required.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a syntax error and a logic error, giving an example of each.
model: Syntax error: breaks the grammar rules of the language so the program does not run (1), e.g. missing bracket / misspelt keyword (1). Logic error: the program runs but does not do what was intended (1), e.g. using `>` instead of `>=` so a boundary value is treated wrongly (1).
exam.commentary: Four separate marks; students lose the example marks by giving vague examples ('typing it wrong'). Name a concrete error.

home: Write a short algorithm (5–8 lines) with **one deliberately hidden logic error**. Write its purpose above it. Bring it in; a partner has to find the error by tracing, not by running it.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 5 · explain 12 · try 25 · check 5 · exam 10 · homework 3
misconceptions: Calling every bug a syntax error. Drill the test: does it *run*? If yes, it's logic.
Fixing the symptom (editing the output message) instead of the cause. Try 1C and Try 3 are built to surface this.
'Refine' misread as 'rewrite'. Refinement keeps the algorithm and improves it.
Writing 'change line 4' without the corrected code.
say: 'Does it run? Then the computer is happy and *you* are wrong — logic error.'
'Trace the boundary. Errors live at the edges.'
teacher.skip: Try 4 (error spotter) is good homework. Keep Try 1 — it is the exam question in disguise.
differentiation: Support: give Try 1 with the faulty line highlighted; students only name the error type and write the fix.
Stretch: in Try 2 ask for the average to be rounded to one decimal place and for the algorithm to work for a list of any length (introduce `.length`).

pt.title: Encontrar e corrigir erros em algoritmos
pt.hook: Este programa devia somar cinco preços e imprimir o total. Imprime 0 sempre. Ninguém escreveu nada mal — todas as linhas correm. Então que tipo de erro é? (O `total = 0` está dentro do ciclo.) Hoje: os erros que correm e continuam errados.

p: Um **erro de sintaxe** quebra as regras da linguagem — um parêntesis em falta, `endif` mal escrito, uma string sem aspas a fechar. O programa não corre e o interpretador diz onde. Um **erro de lógica** obedece às regras mas faz a coisa errada — o programa corre e dá uma resposta errada. Ninguém te avisa; descobre-se testando e rastreando.

explain.h: Os erros de lógica preferidos da OCR
list: **Off by one**: `for i = 0 to 9` em vez de `1 to 10`. Sintoma: falta um item ou há um a mais.
**Comparação errada**: `>` em vez de `>=` (o valor-limite falha); `=` em vez de `==`.
**Inicializar no sítio errado**: `total = 0` dentro do ciclo reinicia-o sempre.
**Atualizar a variável errada** ou esquecer de atualizar a variável do `while` (ciclo infinito).
**Operador ou ordem errados**: `DIV` inteiro onde era preciso `/`.
**Ramo em falta**: um `if` sem `else`, e um caso fica sem saída.

p: As perguntas dão um algoritmo «que contém um erro» e pedem para **identificar** a linha e **corrigir**, ou dão a finalidade e pedem para **completar** linhas em falta. Método: lê primeiro a finalidade; rastreia com um valor normal e um valor-limite; a linha onde a tabela discorda da finalidade é o erro. Depois escreve a linha corrigida por completo.

«Refinar» é fazê-lo cumprir melhor a finalidade sem recomeçar: validar a entrada (rejeitar uma nota acima de 100), tratar um caso-limite (lista vazia), usar um ciclo adequado em vez de um número fixo. Diz o que mudaste e porque é uma melhoria.

keyterms.def: Erro que quebra as regras da linguagem; o programa não corre.
Erro que deixa o programa correr mas produz um resultado errado.
Ciclo ou índice que começa ou acaba uma posição antes ou depois do devido.
Melhorar um algoritmo para cumprir melhor a finalidade, p. ex. com validação ou casos-limite.
